title: Redwood discovery: reliability & incident tolerance - Omega Health
summary: Discovery focused on reliability, incident tolerance and failover policies across Redwood hosted, dedicated and private deployments. Customer wanted guarantees on multi-region routing, SLA implications, canary/fallback strategies, and auditability for healthcare workloads.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-06-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Tom (Omega CTO), Aisha (Platform Eng), Ben (Security)
---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for carving out time. quick rollcall?
[00:05] Tom: Tom here, hi Maya. Aisha and Ben are with me.
[00:08] Aisha: hey.
[00:09] Ben: hi all.
[00:12] Carlos: Carlos from Redwood, SE. thanks for having us.
[00:16] Maya: today we want to focus on reliability and incident tolerance — fallback policies, multi-region routing, sla expectations across our hosted/dedicated/private options. high level is fine, we'll get into specifics for a POC if we move forward.
[00:29] Tom: perfect. high level first — our app processes PHI-ish events, so we need low risk of downtime and clear guarantees. curious how Redwood handles region failover and what happens if a model/region goes unhealthy.
[00:41] Carlos: sure. short answer: we offer routing policies that can failover by policy, by latency threshold, or by model health. in hosted we have a global control plane that can route traffic to another region or to a compatible model variant. for Dedicated you can configure dedicated pools in multiple regions or have a primary region + failover. for Private we support your VPCs and you control routing; we provide the orchestrator hooks.
[01:06] Tom: couple clarifying q's — what's the path during an incident? do you do automatic fallback to a smaller model or route to another region? what's the expected impact to latency and to cost?
[01:18] Maya: great question. typical strategies are: 1) multi-region failover (route to same model in another region), 2) model degradation fallback (route to a cheaper/quantized model variant), 3) capacity-tier fallback (route to a best-effort hosted pool). we can compose these with priority rules. latency impact depends — cross-region adds RTT, model fallback reduces compute latency but may change quality. cost effects vary. we'll show numbers in the POC.
[01:45] Aisha: how automatic is it? we need something that degrades gracefully without manual intervention during nights.
[01:51] Carlos: you can make it fully automatic with health checks and thresholds. e.g., if p95 latency > X ms for 2 minutes or error rate > Y, it triggers a policy: first try another region, if that fails, fallback to compatible model, then to best-effort pool. logs and tracing show the path each request took. you can also set alerts and automated rollbacks.
[02:12] Ben: from a compliance perspective we need to know where data flows. does multi-region routing move PHI outside of our allowed geography?
[02:19] Maya: with Hosted we can pin regioning — we have region controls and data residency options. for strict controls, Dedicated or Private are recommended: Dedicated can be provisioned in a region and have restricted cross-region failover only if you opt-in; Private keeps traffic in your VPC. we'll document legal and technical controls.
[02:36] Tom: SLA — what do we get for hosted vs dedicated? and what's the typical MTTR in incidents?
[02:42] Carlos: Hosted has our standard SLA (we'll send exact numbers in the pack) — it's production-grade but multi-tenant. Dedicated comes with a stronger SLA: committed throughput and latency SLOs with credits for breach. MTTR depends on incident type; for regional infrastructure issues, automatic failovers are sub-minute to couple minutes for traffic cutover, but full remediation can vary. we instrument for detection and aim for low mean time to detect, and for software-level incidents we have hot patches and rollbacks.
[03:07] Aisha: "sub-minute" feels optimistic. can you give a realistic timeline? we need to set expectations internally.
[03:13] Carlos: fair. in practice: detection within 30-90s depending on telemetry, automated routing within 60-180s, so your service could see brief elevated latency during cutover. if a model itself is unhealthy, fallback to a variant can be immediate if we have warmed caches; otherwise there is the cold start of a model instance which is longer. Dedicated with reserved warm instances reduces that cold start significantly.
[03:39] Tom: what about canary rollouts and gradual degradations? we run daily deploys and don't want a bad model change to take us down.
[03:47] Maya: Redwood supports canary and A/B rollouts at the route level. you can stage traffic, monitor quality and latency; automatic rollback rules can trigger on quality regressions (we integrate eval metrics) or on infra signals. for private/dedicated you can pin model versions and do staged rollouts in your environment.
[04:04] Ben: auditability — we need immutable logs showing which model served each request, region, and decision flow for audits.
[04:11] Carlos: yes we capture per-request routing metadata, model version, region, and the chain of fallback decisions. logs can be pulled into your SIEM or exported to a bucket; we also support long retention as an add-on. encryption at rest and KMS integration are supported.
[04:28] Tom: ok. one of our big constraints is cost vs reliability. we might be ok with slightly higher latency but can't multiply costs. what are common patterns to optimize for that?
[04:38] Maya: folks use a mix: keep a low-cost quantized variant for fallback to preserve availability without paying top-tier model costs; use caching/prefix caching for common prompts; and route high-value traffic to dedicated pools while sending best-effort traffic to hosted. Redwood Optimize suggestions can recommend quantization and batching settings by workload.
[04:57] Aisha: about batching — do automatic batching impact latency SLOs? we have some tail-sensitive endpoints.
[05:03] Carlos: we do continuous batching but it's latency-aware: we won't batch beyond a threshold for low-latency routes, and you can set per-route max-batch-delay. so you get throughput improvements without violating tail latency targets.
[05:16] [05:16] Speaker 1: (mumble) question about KV cache during failover?
[05:20] Carlos: good point. KV cache is per-region instance; on cross-region failover you may lose local KV cache which can increase token overhead for a warmup period. we have strategies: replicate hot prefixes or warm caches in target region for critical flows during POC. Dedicated or Private with multi-region replication plan reduces the impact.
[05:41] Tom: can you quantify risk: in a full region outage, what's the expected degradation for our service if we implement multi-region failover plus model fallback?
[05:50] Maya: rough estimate: initial elevated latency while traffic shifts (extra RTT) for maybe 1-3 minutes, plus some increased 95/99 latency if KV cache warms up. quality impact if falling back to quantized model might be slight depending on prompt. cost increases depend on cross-region egress and peak capacity in target region. we'll run a sim during the POC and give concrete numbers.
[06:12] Aisha: security question: for hosted failover, does cross-region routing send unencrypted payloads to other regions?
[06:19] Carlos: all data is encrypted in transit and at rest. cross-region still uses TLS and we can show the cert/key flow. if you need end-to-end control, Private is recommended.
[06:28] Ben: on incident reporting — do you provide post-incident reports? we need RCA and timeline for third-party vendors.
[06:34] Maya: yes for Dedicated and Private we include incident reports for SLA incidents. hosted customers can request detailed logs; enterprise tiers get structured RCA and joint postmortems if engaged.
[06:45] Tom: great. how do we simulate failovers? we want to test both region outage and model degradation in a controlled way.
[06:52] Carlos: we run chaos tests in the POC: we can inject latency, kill model instances, simulate region failover and observe routing. we'll provide a test harness and dashboards.
[07:02] Aisha: ok will need to coordinate windows. also want readout on cost models for running warm instances for failover.
[07:09] Maya: understood. we'll include cost delta estimates for warm standby vs on-demand fallback.
[07:15] [07:15] Tom: any known gaps? like features you don't have yet that we should be aware of?
[07:20] Carlos: one limitation is cross-region KV cache replication is not fully turnkey; we have patterns and managed options but full real-time replication is an advanced setup. also some regulatory data residency automated workflows for cross-border failover require explicit opt-in. we surface those in the security pack.
[07:39] Ben: noted. on compliance, we'll want the SOC2 docs and encryption diagrams.
[07:43] Maya: we'll send those.
[07:45] Carlos: quick note on canary quality checks — we can wire your eval prompts to automatically block rollouts if hallucination or token-cost regressions exceed thresholds.
[07:56] Aisha: cool. about private deployment — if we go that route, what is the ops overhead?
[08:02] Maya: Private is heavier: you manage network and hardware but we provide the control plane and deployment artifacts. many customers start on Hosted or Dedicated then transition to Private for strict compliance.
[08:14] Tom: timeline wise — we want a pilot within 2-3 weeks and then a 6-8 week evaluation. is that feasible?
[08:21] Carlos: feasible. we can spin a small Dedicated pool or do Hosted with region pinning for the pilot. pilot run should include automated failovers and chaos tests.
[08:31] Maya: next steps: we'll send pricing & security pack, Carlos will share runbooks and canary docs, and we'll schedule the POC kickoff.
[08:39] Tom: thanks — please include a sample SLA and the incident playbook.
[08:42] Maya: will do. anything else from you Ben or Aisha?
[08:46] Ben: no that's good.
[08:47] Aisha: all set.
[08:48] Maya: great thanks all.
---

- Redwood to send pricing, Dedicated config options, and security pack (SOC2, KMS notes)
